bibliographic.title: Algorithmic Profiling of Job Seekers in Austria: How Austerity Politics Are Made Effective
bibliographic.authors: Doris Allhutter; Florian Cech; Fabian Fischer; Gabriel Grill; Astrid Mager
bibliographic.citation_apa: Allhutter, D., Cech, F., Fischer, F., Grill, G., & Mager, A. (2020). Algorithmic profiling of job seekers in Austria: How austerity politics are made effective. Frontiers in Big Data, 3, Article 5. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdata.2020.00005

methodology.method_family: qualitative document analysis grounded in science and technology studies and critical data studies
methodology.study_design: in-depth analysis of technical documentation and policy documents
methodology.sample_description: technical documentation and policy documents related to the Austrian Public Employment Service (AMS) algorithmic profiling system
methodology.technology_context: machine learning-based statistical profiling/classification system for job seekers at AMS; not a conversational or generative AI system

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The study analyzes a pre-LLM machine learning profiling algorithm in public employment services and does not address conversational AI, chatbots, agents, or LLM-based systems relevant to conversational governance.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the paper strongly addresses fairness, accountability, transparency, oversight, bias, and regulated public-sector algorithmic governance, it concerns a batch classification/profiling system built on machine learning rather than conversational or LLM-based interaction. The provided text contains no evidence of chatbots, dialogue systems, agents, RAG, guardrails, or generative AI governance, so it falls outside the core scope of a systematic review on conversational governance in LLM systems.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Technology mismatch is explicit in the supplied text: AMS algorithmic profiling via machine learning, with zero conversational-AI evidence.

appraisal.notes: Methodologically sound qualitative STS/critical data studies analysis for its own research question, but not designed to inform conversational or LLM governance mechanisms.

cerqual.explanation: Findings on accountability, transparency, and bias in public-sector algorithmic profiling are coherent and adequately supported for that topic, but relevance to conversational governance in LLM systems is very low because the system studied is neither conversational nor LLM-based.

coding.theme: Politics and governance of algorithmic profiling in public employment services
coding.subtheme: Transparency, accountability, and explainability limits of ML profiling systems

synthesis.main_claim: The AMS job-seeker profiling algorithm coproduces semi-automated managerial practices and austerity politics, while its design, documentation, and implementation raise serious questions about transparency, accountability, objectivity, and possible bias.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a critical qualitative analysis of how technical affordances, social values, and policy goals shape a public-sector machine learning profiling system, with explicit attention to FAT concerns and organizational integration.
synthesis.limitations: No conversational or LLM context; reliance on available technical and policy documents; Austrian AMS-specific case; exact data origins and full technical details not publicly available.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude from central conversational-LLM governance synthesis; at most retain as peripheral foundational context on public-sector algorithmic accountability if the review includes a broad pre-LLM governance background section.
